whatTheFirstRunFound.event: the widened extractor failed its own clean arm on first run
whatTheFirstRunFound.rawFailure: AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: Expected values to be strictly deep-equal: actual: [ 'max', 'presented' ], expected: []
whatTheFirstRunFound.diagnosis: a FALSE POSITIVE in my instrument, not a product defect. The widened classList extractor pulled every quoted literal from every argument, but classList.toggle(cls, force) takes a class name only in its first argument. web/app.js:322-323 calls classList.toggle("is-presented", state === "presented") and classList.toggle("is-max", state === "max"), so the state values 'presented' and 'max' read as class names.
whatTheFirstRunFound.fix: per-method DOM semantics rather than a blanket rule: add() and remove() take a class name in EVERY argument, so classList.remove("is-presented", "is-max") at app.js:422 still contributes both; toggle() contributes only its first argument.
whatTheFirstRunFound.whyNotExcluded: the dispatch forbids adding exclusions and a false positive in the instrument is not a stray in the product. Excluding 'max' and 'presented' would have shipped a gate that quietly ignores two real class-shaped tokens forever.
whatTheFirstRunFound.meaning: the clean arm caught a defect in the instrument being built to run it, on its first execution. That is the arm working and it is the argument for arm A and arm B living in the same test.

adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.question: can the hardened gate be passed by a screen that ships a new class?
adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.answer: not through any of the five scanned sources, proven by ten injected arms. It CAN still be passed by a class assigned through a function argument — web/app.js:690-691 passes "id" and "subj" to a td(text, className) helper. Both happen to be defined classes so nothing strays today. The WDLL names this extractor blindness as explicitly out of scope, so it is recorded rather than fixed.

adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.question: is the derivation genuinely derived, or hardcoded wearing a derivation's clothes?
adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.answer: genuinely derived: the scan reads whatever server.mjs serves. The hardcoded lists in the second test are TRIPWIRES on that derivation, not its input — they fail when the served set changes, which is the point. The call-site count assertion is what stops the derivation silently matching nothing.

adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.question: does anything here become permanently red?
adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.answer: no. The suite is 186 of 186 green on the branch and CI conclusion is 'success'. The tripwires fail only on a real change to the served set, which is a decision someone should make.

adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.question: what did I find that nobody asked about?
adversarialReviewOfTheDeliverable.answer: src/city-identity.test.mjs:184 is a second, weaker implementation of the same rule with the identical comment hole. Measured: with class="hidden" injected into index.html only ui.test.mjs fires; city-identity.test.mjs stays green. Left untouched as outside this item's named scope; reported in the close and in the PR body as a finding with a concrete recommendation.
